propositions.text: This is an application for judicial review under subsection 72(1) of the IRPA of the RPD decision dated February 29, 2016.
propositions.quote: This is an application for judicial review under subsection 72(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c. 27 (IRPA), of the decision dated February 29, 2016, in which the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) of the Immigration and Refugee Board found that the applicant was not a refugee nor a person in need of protection under sections 96 and 97 of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The court states this is a judicial review application of the RPD decision dated February 29, 2016, under subsection 72(1) of the IRPA.

propositions.text: The applicant is a 27-year-old Cuban citizen of Yoruba faith with a son in Cuba and a spouse and daughter in Canada.
propositions.quote: The applicant, age 27, is a citizen of Cuba and of Yoruba faith. He has a seven-year-old son, who lives in Cuba. He also has a spouse and a three-year-old daughter, who are both Canadian citizens.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant is a 27-year-old Cuban citizen of Yoruba faith with family in Cuba and Canada, says the court.

propositions.text: The applicant alleges political persecution in Cuba starting in 2007 after defending his mother from police harassment.
propositions.quote: The applicant alleges that he faces political persecution in Cuba. Since 2005, his mother has been involved with the Ladies in White, a peaceful movement opposing the imprisonment of Cuban political dissidents. His problems allegedly began in 2007, when he reportedly defended his mother when police officers came to arrest and harass her at her home. He says he was arrested as well, detained for 24 hours, and questioned.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant alleges political persecution in Cuba since 2007 after defending his mother, says the applicant.

propositions.text: The applicant lost his teaching job in 2008 due to opposition to the Cuban regime and faced ongoing economic hardship and harassment.
propositions.quote: In December 2008, the applicant reportedly lost his job as a physical education teacher in a school in due to his opposition to the Cuban regime. Ostracized by the government, he was never again able to work in his field and was unable to find another job. In April 2015, a short period of employment in a factory with difficult working conditions ended in the applicant being dismissed without having been paid, for political reasons. He was living off the food bank and an illegal food and cold drink business, since he was unable to obtain a permit. This business was often discovered by the authorities, who would confiscate his property and cash, in addition to charging fines.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant alleges job loss and economic hardship due to political opposition, says the applicant.

propositions.text: The applicant alleges a failed boat escape attempt in 2010, followed by detention and surveillance by Cuban authorities.
propositions.quote: On January 1, 2010, the applicant says he attempted to escape Cuba by boat, in vain, as he was intercepted by the coast guard. He was allegedly detained for over a month, then released under strict surveillance.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant alleges a failed escape attempt and detention in 2010, says the applicant.

propositions.text: The applicant alleges being questioned by authorities after visits by his spouse to Cuba, whom he has known since childhood.
propositions.quote: The applicant and his spouse have known each other since childhood. They began a romantic relationship during one of her stays in Cuba in 2012, and they had a daughter in 2013. The applicant was allegedly questioned by the authorities after each visit by his spouse to Cuba.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant alleges questioning by authorities after spouse's visits to Cuba, says the applicant.

propositions.text: The applicant left Cuba for Ecuador in October 2015 with spouse's help, traveled through eight countries, and claimed refugee protection in Canada in December 2015.
propositions.quote: The applicant apparently got a passport and left Cuba for Ecuador a few months later, on October 21, 2015, with the help of his spouse. After crossing eight countries, he reached Canada on December 9, 2015, and claimed refugee protection. He was taken in by his spouse’s family.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant left Cuba in 2015, traveled through eight countries, and claimed refugee protection in Canada, says the court.

propositions.text: The applicant attempted suicide in December 2015, was hospitalized, then found himself isolated and without representation before the RPD hearing in February 2016.
propositions.quote: The applicant attempted suicide on December 30, 2015, feeling alone and fearing he would be deported to Cuba. He was released from hospital on January 4, 2016, and found himself on the streets, isolated, unable to return to his in-laws. His first attorney stopped representing him on Friday, February 12, 2016. The hearing before the RPD was held with a new attorney representing the applicant on February 16, 2016.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant attempted suicide, was hospitalized, isolated, and changed attorneys before the RPD hearing, says the court.

propositions.text: The RPD refused refugee protection, finding the applicant not credible due to omissions, contradictions, and inconsistencies.
propositions.quote: On February 29, 2016, the RPD refused the applicant’s claim for refugee protection on the grounds that he was not a refugee or a person in need of protection. The RPD found that the applicant was not credible, noting several omissions, contradictions, and inconsistencies in his testimony.

propositions.text: The RPD found the applicant unable to identify the human rights organization, omitted information in his BOC form, and contradicted himself on detentions and jobs.
propositions.quote: It found that the applicant was unable to identify the human rights organization with which his persecutors allegedly associated him, that he left certain information out of his Basis of Claim (BOC) form, and that he contradicted himself on the number of times he was detained and the number of jobs he held in Cuba.

propositions.text: The RPD was unconvinced the applicant was under close surveillance, noting he obtained a passport and left Cuba without inconvenience.
propositions.quote: The panel was not convinced that the applicant was under close surveillance by the Cuban authorities, as he claims, since he was able to obtain a passport and leave Cuba for Ecuador without being inconvenienced.

propositions.text: The RPD concluded the applicant did not have the profile of a persecuted dissident or counter-revolutionary.
propositions.quote: To summarize, the RPD found that the applicant did not have the profile of a dissident or a counter-revolutionary persecuted by the Cuban authorities.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD refused protection, finding the applicant not credible and lacking a persecuted dissident profile, says the RPD.

propositions.text: The applicant argues the RPD's credibility analysis is unreasonable, focusing on presentation over merits and ignoring explanations.
propositions.quote: The applicant argues that the RPD’s analysis of his credibility is unreasonable. Although he admits his testimony may have had omissions and contradictions, he argues the RPD focused on the presentation rather than the merits of the case and ignored his explanations.

propositions.text: The applicant claims the RPD misinterpreted his story and was unaware of translation and interpretation misunderstandings.
propositions.quote: He says the RPD misinterpreted his story and was unaware of the misunderstandings that can occur in translation and simultaneous interpretation.

propositions.text: The applicant claims the RPD lacked openness and sensitivity given his psychological instability and attorney withdrawal before the hearing.
propositions.quote: The applicant also claims the RPD lacked openness and sensitivity, considering that he was psychologically unstable when he filled out his BOC form and that his first attorney withdrew from the case a few days before the hearing.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues the RPD's credibility analysis was unreasonable, misinterpreted his story, and lacked sensitivity, says the applicant.

propositions.text: The respondent argues the RPD's credibility finding is reasonable given omissions and contradictions in evidence.
propositions.quote: The respondent argues that the RPD’s finding that the applicant lacks credibility is reasonable. Given the omissions, inconsistencies, and contradictions in the evidence, the RPD was fully within its rights in making negative inferences about the applicant’s credibility.

propositions.text: The respondent argues the applicant was fit to appear at the hearing despite psychological state, supported by hospitalization statement.
propositions.quote: As for the applicant’s psychological state, the respondent argues that he presented a hospitalization statement indicating that he was fit to appear at the hearing.

propositions.text: The respondent argues the RPD showed openness and sensitivity by allowing additional documents after the hearing.
propositions.quote: The RPD argues that it demonstrated openness and sensitivity by allowing the attorney to file additional documents and written submissions after the hearing.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent argues the RPD's credibility finding is reasonable and showed openness despite applicant's psychological state, says the respondent.

propositions.text: The issue is whether the RPD erred in finding the applicant lacked credibility, a fact question under reasonableness review.
propositions.quote: The issue in this case is as follows: did the RPD err in finding that the applicant lacked credibility? This is a question of fact subject to the reasonableness standard of review.

propositions.text: The court must defer to the RPD's credibility assessment as a specialized panel (Khosa, 2009 SCC 12, para 89).
propositions.quote: The Court must show deference to the assessment of the applicant’s credibility by the specialized panel that is the RPD (Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v. Khosa, [2009] 1 SCR 339, 2009 SCC 12, at paragraph 89).

paragraphs.summary: The issue is whether the RPD erred in credibility finding, reviewed for reasonableness with deference, says the court.

propositions.text: The RPD erred in assessing the applicant's credibility and made an unreasonable decision.
propositions.quote: Based on a study of the file and a close reading of the hearing transcript, it appears that the RPD erred in its assessment of the applicant’s credibility and that it rendered an unreasonable decision concerning him.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RPD erred and made an unreasonable credibility decision.

propositions.text: The RPD questioned the applicant's claim of targeting by Cuban authorities due to communication problems in testimony.
propositions.quote: The RPD questioned the applicant’s claims that he was targeted by the Cuban authorities, who associate him with the Ladies in White and a human rights organization whose name he does not know. In the applicant’s testimony, it was clear that there was a communication problem: [translation] Q. So I asked you why would the Cuban authorities put you in prison, do you think? A. Because they say I belong to human rights. Q. Does this organization have a name? A. No, human rights. Q. So, do you—what are being accused of, concretely? A. Belonging to human rights. Q. So, human rights is an organization with no name? A. Just human rights, I know them as human rights. Q. Who are these people? A. They are people who are fighting for human rights in Cuba. Q. Do they have names? A. Human rights. Q. That’s rights; that’s the official name, human rights? A. I don’t know. I just know it as human rights. Q. And how many of them are there? A. I don’t know. A lot of people. Q. Do you know these people? A. No. […] Q. So the Ladies in White are not a human rights organization? A. They’re also related to human rights. Q. But it’s not the organization you were talking about earlier? A. I don’t understand. Q. You told me you were being associated with an organization called human rights. A. Yes. Q. So they are not the Ladies in White? A. Well, the Ladies in White are the Ladies in White, and human rights are human rights. Just the Ladies in White are associated with human rights people. […] (Excerpts from the transcription of the February 16, 2016, hearing, at pages 24–25.)

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RPD questioned the applicant's targeting claim due to communication problems in testimony.

propositions.text: The RPD erred by requiring the applicant to name a specific organization when he is not a member and was targeted due to his mother's activism.
propositions.quote: While the applicant says he was targeted by the Cuban authorities because they associate him with the human rights movement in general, the RPD requires him to name a specific organization. But the applicant is not a member of such an organization, which he repeats many times. At most, he says the authorities target him because his mother belongs to the Ladies in White. In making a negative inference about the applicant’s credibility based on this aspect of his testimony, the RPD made a decisive error of fact, based on his psychological situation (see also a document from Quebec emergency social services that was to be read in its entirety, which stated that the applicant was homeless for some time and described his situation as precarious).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RPD erred by requiring a specific organization name and made a decisive error on credibility.

propositions.text: Other omissions and contradictions do not excessively undermine credibility and can be explained by exhaustion and translation loss.
propositions.quote: Otherwise, the other omissions and contradictions found by the RPD in the applicant’s story do not excessively undermine his credibility. Seen in isolation, the applicant’s faults are of little importance and can be explained by his exhaustion after travelling across the continent for approximately two months before filling out his BOC form in Canada and by the loss of information in translation.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds other faults do not excessively undermine credibility and are explainable.

propositions.text: The RPD’s decision should be set aside and returned to a differently constituted panel.
propositions.quote: Consequently, the RPD’s decision should be set aside and returned to a differently constituted panel.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the RPD decision should be set aside and reconsidered by a different panel.

propositions.text: The judicial review application is allowed, the RPD decision is set aside, and the matter is returned for reconsideration by a different panel.
propositions.quote: The application for judicial review is allowed and the RPD’s February 29, 2016, decision is set aside. JUDGMENT THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that the application for judicial review is allowed and the RPD’s February 29, 2016, decision is set aside. The matter is returned to the RPD before a differently constituted panel for reconsideration.

propositions.text: No questions of general importance are certified.
propositions.quote: There are no questions of general importance to be certified.

paragraphs.summary: The court allows the judicial review, sets aside the RPD decision, returns the matter for reconsideration, and declines certification.
